title: Awakening ImageCAS: Open Coronary Ostia and Centerlines for CCTA
partialText:
AI-assistance disclosure: I drafted this article with AI assistance, then edited it and fact-checked every number against the paper (arXiv:2611.09714).

Anyone who has built a coronary CT angiography (CCTA) workflow knows where the coronary tree starts: at the two ostia, where the left and right coronary arteries leave the aortic root. Curved planar reformation, vessel tracking, branch labeling and stenosis measurement all hang off that point and off the centerline that grows from it. Public data for training a model to find those points has been thin. In arXiv:2611.09714, Matteo Leccardi and colleagues at Politecnico di Milano, with ETH Zurich and the University of Pavia, fix that for ImageCAS, the largest public coronary segmentation dataset. The project is called Awakening ImageCAS.

What they released

The release has three parts, all tied to the 1000 CCTA scans of ImageCAS (Guangdong Provincial People’s Hospital, 2012 to 2018):

  • Ostium labels for every scan. A left and a right ostium for all 1000 patients, each stored in world (RAS, mm) and voxel coordinates with the affine matrices, plus a 3D Slicer markup per scan.
  • Rooted centerline graphs. One connected tree per side for 999 of the 1000 patients, grown from the annotated ostia along the official ImageCAS masks. Every node carries position, lumen radius, topological type and side. Files come as networkx-compatible GML, VTK polydata and Slicer markups, with a per-case quality table.
  • Open-weight ostium localizers. Four of six benchmarked 3D models (SwinUNETR-V2, nnResUNet, ResNet50, ResNet101), plus a SwinUNETR-V2 trained at 1.0 mm spacing, with MIT-licensed inference and training code.

Before this, the only CCTA data with ostium information were CAT08 and ASOCA, 72 scans in total, where the ostium is only implicit as a centerline start point. CAT08 can no longer be downloaded from an official source. No dedicated ostium localizer had been released with code or weights.

How the labels were made

The first 500 scans were annotated by three people each, drawn from six trained annotators in rotating groups that reshuffled every 25 images, working in 3D Slicer across axial, coronal and sagittal views. The consensus point is the mean of the three markers, followed by a visual check for gross errors. On these scans an individual annotator sits a mean of 1.45 mm (right) and 1.95 mm (left) from the mean of the other two, so the landmark itself carries a millimeter or two of uncertainty.

The second 500 used a human-in-the-loop pass. A SwinUNETR-V2 trained on the first batch plus CAT08 and ASOCA proposed both ostia, and one annotator reviewed every scan. The reviewer moved the point in 88 scans, and the model missed an ostium in 10, which were placed by hand. That took about 5 person-hours, against roughly 144 person-hours for the triple manual annotation of the first batch. The test set comes only from the first, fully manual batch.

How the centerlines are grown

Instead of thinning the mask into a skeleton, which leaves loops and spurious stubs, the authors resample the mask to 0.5 mm, build a cost that is cheap on the vessel axis and expensive near the wall, and propagate a minimal-cost front from each ostium. The tree then grows by repeatedly tracing the path to the farthest uncovered voxel and keeping it as a branch only if it adds at least 5 mm of new vessel. Because every path comes from the same minimal-path map, the result is a tree by construction. A second pass with a capped wall distance keeps the path centered at bulky bifurcations, and gaps in the mask of up to 10 mm, such as at a severe stenosis, are bridged.

The numbers worth knowing

On 58 held-out scans (50 ImageCAS, 4 ASOCA, 4 CAT08), SwinUNETR-V2 and nnResUNet found every ostium with no error above 5 mm. Median errors were 0.70 to 0.87 mm per side, below the annotators’ own spread. The authors read that as agreement with the reference at the level of a human reader. nnResUNet took 41.1 s per scan against 55.6 s for SwinUNETR-V2 on an A100, including loading and export.

The data matter more than the architecture. Trained on CAT08 and ASOCA alone, SwinUNETR-V2 failed on 34% of right and 53% of left ostia. Adding 250 ImageCAS scans removed every failure. The centerline method, checked on the 40 ASOCA scans where reference centerlines come from the same masks, covers a median 99.5% of the reference length at a median 0.22 mm from it.

What it hangs on a scan in a viewer

Run the localizer on a CCTA volume and you get two points, R and L, in the image’s own world coordinates and as continuous voxel indices, written as JSON and as a Slicer point list. Pair those with your own coronary segmentation and the released extraction procedure, and you have two rooted trees with a radius at every node. In a DICOM viewer that maps to two ostium markers on the aortic root, a seed for automatic vessel tracking, a centerline overlay you can drive a curved planar reformation along, and a radius profile per branch for a first-pass stenosis view. For a planning tool, the ostium height above the valve annulus is a TAVI risk measurement that needs exactly this landmark.

One practical gotcha is the coordinate frame. All coordinates are RAS, the convention of nibabel, MONAI and Slicer. ITK, SimpleITK and DICOM patient coordinates use LPS, so x and y flip sign. Get that wrong and your markers land in the wrong place.

Why a clinical AI team should care

  • A shared benchmark. The test split, weights and a grading scheme (Optimal, Good, Acceptable, Failed, with thresholds from ostial anatomy and annotator spread) are public, so you can compare an in-house localizer on the same 58 scans.
  • Cheap extension. The second batch shows that model-proposed points plus one reviewer cost a few hours per 500 scans. The released models can seed the same loop on your own data.
  • Spacing rules you can use. Training and running at 1.0 mm keeps accuracy and roughly halves time (21.9 s for SwinUNETR-V2). Running a 0.5 mm model on a 1.0 mm volume breaks it, with 22.4% of left ostia failing, so resample to the training spacing.

Where it falls short

  • ImageCAS is a single hospital. CAT08 and ASOCA add only 72 scans, so per-dataset numbers are fragile, and the models have not been validated clinically or prospectively.
  • The labels assume one ostium per side. Separate LAD and circumflex ostia, a single coronary ostium and anomalous origins are not represented, and model behavior on them is unknown. That is a gap for a tool that wants to flag anomalous origins.
  • Annotators were biomedical engineers, not clinicians, and the second 500 labels came from one reviewer correcting model output without independent verification.
  • The centerlines inherit ImageCAS mask defects. One patient has no right tree because the mask never reaches the ostium. Visual review confirmed missed small distal branches in 29 patients, and in 12 of the 25 patients where left and right masks touch, a distal segment went to the wrong tree.
  • Trained on ImageCAS alone, the models still transferred to CAT08 and ASOCA, but with isolated failures on the order of a hundred millimeters, meaning the network locked onto a different structure. Any viewer integration should sanity-check the distance between the two ostia (33 mm on average in this data) before trusting the points.
  • Only gated CCTA was tested. Non-gated aortic CT is left for future work.

Code, weights and license

The code for training, inference and evaluation, with the train, validation and test lists, is on GitHub at AAMIASoftwares-research/HCATOstiaLocalizationRelease under the MIT license. Inference takes NIfTI or NRRD, reorients to RAS, resamples, clips to -200 to 800 HU and runs a sliding window, so you do not have to preprocess. The ostium and centerline annotations are on Zenodo (10.5281/zenodo.23243093) and the weights in a separate Zenodo record (10.5281/zenodo.23399623), both under CC BY-NC 4.0, matching the non-commercial terms of ImageCAS itself. No CT images or masks are redistributed. You download ImageCAS separately. For a product team, the code is free to reuse, but the annotations and weights are research-only unless you get permission, so a commercial ostium detector would need retraining on data you are allowed to use. The release is research software and is not a medical device.

Paper: arXiv:2611.09714 · Project: hal9000-lab.github.io/Awakening-ImageCAS · Code: GitHub (MIT) · Data and weights: Zenodo (CC BY-NC 4.0)

title: How to Upgrade Kafka Consumers to KIP-848: Faster Rebalances, Safe Commits and Idempotent Writes
partialText:
A Hands-On Java Guide to the Consumer Group Protocol, Server-Side Assignors and a Rolling Migration Without Downtime

For most of Kafka’s history, every consumer group rebalance has been a small stop-the-world event. One instance restarts, a pod gets rescheduled or you scale from six consumers to eight, and the whole group pauses while the members agree on a new assignment. In a busy system that pause shows up as lag spikes, duplicate processing and on-call pages that say “consumer lag high” at 3 a.m. for no obvious reason.

The fix has been production ready since Apache Kafka 4.0: the new consumer group protocol from KIP-848, which moves assignment to the broker and makes rebalances incremental. The catch is that it is still opt-in for the Java client, some familiar configs now throw an exception, and faster rebalances do nothing for you if your commits and writes are not safe. In this guide I walk through how the new protocol works, a production-style Java consumer that commits correctly and writes idempotently, a rolling migration plan and the pitfalls that catch teams out.

The Problem

Under the classic protocol, the group coordinator on the broker only tracks membership. The actual partition assignment is computed on the client side by one elected group leader. When membership changes, members rejoin through a JoinGroup and SyncGroup round trip, and with the default eager assignors every member gives up all of its partitions until the new assignment arrives. Cooperative rebalancing improved this by revoking only the partitions that move, but it still needs multiple rounds and still depends on every member reaching a global synchronization point.

That design creates three recurring problems in production:

  • Group-wide pauses: a single slow or misbehaving member can hold up a rebalance for everyone else.
  • Duplicates: records processed but not committed before a revocation are processed again by the new owner.
  • Complex clients: because the assignment logic lives in every client library, behavior differs between Java, librdkafka and other clients, and upgrades are risky.

Core Concepts

KIP-848 keeps the consumer API almost the same but changes who does the work. According to the Apache Kafka documentation, the design is fully incremental and no longer relies on a global synchronization barrier.

  • The broker computes the assignment: the group coordinator runs a server-side assignor and sends each member only the partitions it should add or remove. Members that are not affected keep consuming.
  • Everything happens over heartbeats: instead of JoinGroup and SyncGroup, each consumer sends a ConsumerGroupHeartbeat request. The response carries assignment changes, so there is no separate rebalance phase.
  • Two built-in assignors: the broker ships with uniform, the default, and range. A client can request one with group.remote.assignor. Classic RangeAssignor maps to range, while CooperativeStickyAssignor, StickyAssignor and RoundRobinAssignor map to uniform.
  • Timeouts move to the server: the broker configs group.consumer.session.timeout.ms (default 45 seconds) and group.consumer.heartbeat.interval.ms (default 5 seconds) replace the client-side settings. max.poll.interval.ms stays on the client.
  • Static membership still works: setting group.instance.id lets a restarting consumer rejoin with its old identity, and the AWS Big Data Blog notes that short restarts within the session timeout do not trigger a reassignment.

The timeline matters for planning. The protocol was early access in 3.7 and became generally available in 4.0. KIP-1274, now accepted, makes the new protocol the default for KafkaConsumer in Kafka 5.0 and removes classic support from KafkaConsumer in 6.0. Since 4.3, a consumer that still uses the classic protocol logs a message recommending the switch. The latest release, Kafka 4.4.0, shipped on October 22, as summarized in Red Hat’s Kafka monthly digest.

Step 1: Check the Brokers

The new protocol is enabled on the server automatically since 4.0 and controlled by the group.version feature flag. Confirm the feature is finalized before touching any consumer:

bin/kafka-features.sh --bootstrap-server kafka:9092 describe
# look for: Feature: group.version  FinalizedVersionLevel: 1 (or higher)

If you run a managed service, check that your provider’s Kafka version supports the consumer protocol. If group.version is missing or finalized at 0, upgrade the feature with kafka-features.sh before going further.

Step 2: Configure the Java Consumer

Here is a consumer configuration for a service called orders-projector that reads an orders topic and maintains a read model in PostgreSQL. It uses Java 21 and the Kafka 4.4 client.

Properties props = new Properties();
props.put(ConsumerConfig.BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS_CONFIG, "kafka:9092");
props.put(ConsumerConfig.GROUP_ID_CONFIG, "orders-projector");
props.put(ConsumerConfig.GROUP_PROTOCOL_CONFIG, "consumer");          // opt in to KIP-848
props.put(ConsumerConfig.GROUP_REMOTE_ASSIGNOR_CONFIG, "uniform");    // optional, uniform is the default
props.put(ConsumerConfig.GROUP_INSTANCE_ID_CONFIG, System.getenv("POD_NAME")); // static membership
props.put(ConsumerConfig.ENABLE_AUTO_COMMIT_CONFIG, false);
props.put(ConsumerConfig.AUTO_OFFSET_RESET_CONFIG, "earliest");
props.put(ConsumerConfig.MAX_POLL_RECORDS_CONFIG, 200);
props.put(ConsumerConfig.MAX_POLL_INTERVAL_MS_CONFIG, 300_000);      // still client side
props.put(ConsumerConfig.KEY_DESERIALIZER_CLASS_CONFIG, StringDeserializer.class);
props.put(ConsumerConfig.VALUE_DESERIALIZER_CLASS_CONFIG, StringDeserializer.class);
// Do NOT set session.timeout.ms, heartbeat.interval.ms or partition.assignment.strategy

That last comment is not a style tip. In the Kafka client source, ConsumerConfig checks for these keys when the consumer protocol is selected and throws a ConfigException saying they cannot be set. A config file copied from an old service will fail at startup, which is good, because it fails loudly instead of silently ignoring your timeout.

If you use Spring Boot, the same settings go under spring.kafka.consumer.properties, for example group.protocol set to consumer. Remove any session timeout or assignment strategy entries from your application properties at the same time.

Step 3: Commit Safely With a Rebalance Listener

Faster rebalances reduce how often partitions move, but partitions still move. Each time one does, any record you processed and did not commit will be processed again by the next owner. The standard defense is to track the last processed offset per partition, commit asynchronously during normal operation and commit synchronously for exactly the partitions being revoked.

public final class OrderProjector implements ConsumerRebalanceListener, Runnable {
    private final KafkaConsumer<String, String> consumer;
    private final OrderViewStore store;
    private final Map<TopicPartition, OffsetAndMetadata> processed = new HashMap<>();
    private volatile boolean running = true;
    public OrderProjector(Properties props, OrderViewStore store) {
        this.consumer = new KafkaConsumer<>(props);
        this.store = store;
    }
    @Override
    public void onPartitionsRevoked(Collection<TopicPartition> partitions) {
        Map<TopicPartition, OffsetAndMetadata> toCommit = new HashMap<>();
        for (TopicPartition tp : partitions) {
            OffsetAndMetadata offset = processed.remove(tp);
            if (offset != null) toCommit.put(tp, offset);
        }
        if (!toCommit.isEmpty()) consumer.commitSync(toCommit);
    }
    @Override
    public void onPartitionsAssigned(Collection<TopicPartition> partitions) {
        log.info("assigned {}", partitions);
    }
    @Override
    public void onPartitionsLost(Collection<TopicPartition> partitions) {
        partitions.forEach(processed::remove);   // too late to commit, another member owns them
    }
    @Override
    public void run() {
        consumer.subscribe(List.of("orders"), this);
        try {
            while (running) {
                ConsumerRecords<String, String> records = consumer.poll(Duration.ofMillis(500));
                for (ConsumerRecord<String, String> record : records) {
                    store.apply(OrderEvent.parse(record.value()));
                    processed.put(new TopicPartition(record.topic(), record.partition()),
                                  new OffsetAndMetadata(record.offset() + 1));
                }
                if (!records.isEmpty()) {
                    consumer.commitAsync(Map.copyOf(processed), (offsets, ex) -> {
                        if (ex != null) log.warn("async commit failed, will retry on next poll", ex);
                    });
                }
            }
        } catch (WakeupException e) {
            // expected on shutdown
        } finally {
            try {
                if (!processed.isEmpty()) consumer.commitSync(processed);
            } finally {
                consumer.close();
            }
        }
    }
    public void shutdown() {
        running = false;
        consumer.wakeup();
    }
}

A few details are worth calling out. Under the consumer protocol, the ConsumerRebalanceListener Javadoc says onPartitionsRevoked is called only with the partitions being revoked, and only when that set is not empty, the same behavior as cooperative rebalancing in the classic protocol. Callbacks run on the consumer thread inside poll, so calling commitSync from them is safe. The committed offset is always the next offset to read, which is why the code stores offset plus one.

onPartitionsLost is different. It fires when the member has already lost ownership, for example after missing heartbeats past the session timeout. Committing there would fail or, worse, overwrite the new owner’s progress, so the code simply drops its local state.

Step 4: Make the Write Idempotent

Even with careful commits, a crash between writing to the database and committing the offset will replay records. At-least-once delivery is the realistic guarantee for a consumer that writes to an external system, so the write itself must tolerate duplicates. For a read model, a version check in an upsert does the job:

INSERT INTO order_view (order_id, status, total_cents, version, updated_at)
VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, now())
ON CONFLICT (order_id) DO UPDATE
SET status      = EXCLUDED.status,
    total_cents = EXCLUDED.total_cents,
    version     = EXCLUDED.version,
    updated_at  = now()
WHERE order_view.version < EXCLUDED.version;

The WHERE clause turns a replayed or out-of-order event into a no-op. The version should come from the producer, such as an aggregate version or the source database’s commit sequence. If you build your topics with change data capture, the source position is a good candidate, which I covered in How to Build Reliable CDC Pipelines With Debezium and Postgres. For events without a natural version, store the event ID in a processed_events table inside the same database transaction as the write and skip IDs you have already seen.

Step 5: Migrate a Running Group Without Downtime

The official documentation describes two upgrade paths. The offline path stops every consumer, waits for the group to become empty and restarts everything with the new protocol, which costs a short outage. The online path is a normal rolling deployment: the group converts from classic to consumer when the first new-protocol member joins, and the coordinator lets both kinds of members work together during the rollout. The broker setting group.consumer.migration.policy controls this and defaults to bidirectional, so you can also roll back the same way.

A safe rollout looks like this:

  1. Remove the classic-only settings first. Delete session.timeout.ms, heartbeat.interval.ms and partition.assignment.strategy from the service config and pick the equivalent server-side assignor.
  2. Move custom timeouts to the group. If you relied on a longer session timeout, set it per group on the broker so it applies to every member.
  3. Deploy one instance with the new protocol. Watch lag and error logs before rolling the rest.
  4. Verify membership and lag. Describe the group and its members to confirm everyone is stable and partitions are spread as expected.
  5. Roll the remaining instances. Keep the rollback path ready until the whole group has run cleanly for a while.

The commands for steps 2 and 4:

bin/kafka-configs.sh --bootstrap-server kafka:9092 --alter --entity-type groups --entity-name orders-projector --add-config consumer.session.timeout.ms=60000
bin/kafka-consumer-groups.sh --bootstrap-server kafka:9092 --describe --group orders-projector --members
bin/kafka-consumer-groups.sh --bootstrap-server kafka:9092 --describe --group orders-projector

The per-group session timeout has to fall between the broker’s group.consumer.min.session.timeout.ms and group.consumer.max.session.timeout.ms, which default to 45 and 60 seconds. If you need more, raise the broker maximum first.

Common Pitfalls

  • Old configs in shared templates: a leftover session.timeout.ms in a base properties file throws a ConfigException at startup. Search every config source, including environment variables and Helm values.
  • Custom client-side assignors: the consumer protocol does not support client-side assignors, and online migration only works when the classic group uses an assignor without custom metadata. Teams with a custom assignor need the offline path or a server-side assignor implementing ConsumerGroupPartitionAssignor.
  • Assuming slow processing is now fine: max.poll.interval.ms still applies. If one batch takes longer than five minutes, the member is still removed. Lower max.poll.records or move heavy work off the poll thread with clear backpressure.
  • Rack-aware assignment: the docs say rack-aware assignment is not fully supported yet. If you depend on it to cut cross-zone traffic, test before migrating.
  • Calling enforceRebalance: both enforceRebalance methods are unsupported with the new protocol, so code that forces rebalances needs another approach.
  • Monitoring blind spots: older tools that inspect groups through classic admin APIs may not show consumer protocol groups properly. Check your lag exporter and dashboards in staging first.
  • Expecting Kafka Streams to follow: Streams has its own rebalance protocol under KIP-1071. This guide applies to plain consumers and frameworks built on KafkaConsumer, such as Spring Kafka.

Best Practices

  1. Migrate one group at a time. Start with a low-risk group, learn what your dashboards show, then move on to critical paths.
  2. Use static membership for stateful or slow-starting services. Map group.instance.id to a stable name such as a StatefulSet pod name so restarts and deployments do not reshuffle partitions.
  3. Commit on revoke, drop on lost. Commit synchronously for revoked partitions, never commit for lost ones and commit asynchronously the rest of the time.
  4. Design for at-least-once. Make every external write idempotent with versions or event IDs. Faster rebalances lower the duplicate rate, but they do not make it zero.
  5. Own timeouts at the group level. Treat session and heartbeat settings as platform configuration on the broker or per group, reviewed like any other infrastructure change.
  6. Alert on time to catch up, not just raw lag. A lag of 50,000 records means very different things for a topic doing 100 records per second and one doing 50,000.
  7. Get ahead of Kafka 5.0. Classic becomes the non-default path in 5.0 and leaves KafkaConsumer in 6.0. Migrating now, on your own schedule, is easier than doing it during a forced upgrade.

Final Thoughts

KIP-848 is one of those changes that looks small in your code, often a single property, and large in production. Moving assignment to the broker and making it incremental removes the group-wide pause that has caused so many lag spikes, and it makes client behavior more consistent across languages. Combined with static membership, a routine deployment of a consumer fleet can now happen without most partitions moving at all.

The protocol does not fix sloppy offset handling or non-idempotent writes, though. The teams that benefit most will pair the migration with the basics: commit on revoke, tolerate replays and watch the right metrics. If you are already running Java services on modern runtimes, the same discipline applies to concurrency, which I covered in How to Run Java Virtual Threads Safely in Spring Boot.

Have you moved any consumer groups to the new protocol yet? Tell me in the comments what changed in your rebalance times and lag, or what is holding your migration back.

Sources: Apache Kafka documentation, Apache Kafka KIP-1274, Apache Kafka source on GitHub, Confluent, Red Hat Developer, AWS Big Data Blog

title: OpenBrain: Brain MRI Parcellations Shipped With a Risk Score
partialText:
AI-assistance disclosure: I drafted this article with AI assistance, then edited it and fact-checked every number against the paper (arXiv:2611.05348).

When we train a brain parcellation model on pseudo-labels, we run FastSurfer or SynthSeg over a few thousand public T1 scans and get a folder of label maps. Somewhere in that folder are cases where the cortex leaks into the skull or the hippocampus is a scatter of fragments. Nobody opens all of them. In arXiv:2611.05348, Qizhen Lan, Yu-Chun Hsu, Yuxiang Wei, Lijing Zhu, Zenan Sun, Liang He, Lishan Yu and Xiaoqian Jiang (The University of Texas Health Science Center at Houston, Georgia Institute of Technology, University of Houston-Clear Lake and ETH Zurich) release OpenBrain, a set of generated whole-brain parcellations where every case ships with the evidence you need to decide whether to trust it. It was accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Evaluations and Datasets track.

What OpenBrain is

OpenBrain covers 35,838 T1-weighted scans drawn from 607 OpenNeuro datasets. Each scan is skull-stripped with SynthStrip, resampled to 1 mm isotropic, and parcellated into 110 regions by ModernSurfer, a 3D residual U-Net trained with nnU-Net v2 on FreeSurfer 7.4.1 labels. That is the primary label. Two more models, SwinUNETR and UNETR, parcellate the same scan, and their outputs are released too. They are there as a committee, so you can see where three different architectures disagree.

The authors describe these as generated labels and say plainly that they are neither manual annotations nor clinical-grade segmentations. The release is organized as case records: each case folder holds the skull-stripped T1, the brain mask, the three parcellations, and a row in a metadata table with the OpenNeuro source, DOI, license, and whatever age, sex and scanner fields the source dataset published.

The seven checks

QC-7 is the piece I would copy. It is a panel of seven reference-free checks run on every case. Three look at label geometry: labels outside the brain mask (Q1), region volumes that are unusual for that source dataset (Q2), and pieces of a region far from its main body (Q3). One checks image-label consistency, meaning how much the T1 intensity varies inside each region (Q4). Three measure committee disagreement: overlap between the primary label and the other two models (Q5), voxel-level vote uncertainty (Q6), and differences in region volumes across the three models (Q7).

Each raw value is turned into a percentile across the release, flipped where needed so that higher always means riskier. The combined risk score R is the plain mean of the seven percentiles. Sort by R and the lowest quarter becomes HighConf, the middle half Standard, and the top quarter Flagged. The raw values are released alongside the tiers, so if you care more about leakage than about committee agreement, you can reweight and re-threshold without rerunning any model.

What it hangs on a scan

Open one case and you get a T1, a 110-label map, two alternative label maps, a voxel-wise disagreement picture you can compute from them, and a bar chart of seven percentiles. In the paper’s figure, the lowest-risk case shows clean labels and only thin entropy along region borders. The highest-risk case has labels scattered across a noisy image, entropy filling the brain, and every bar in the red.

Testing the risk score

The authors froze the checks, the tier cutoffs and the evaluation label set on two development cohorts (IXI and BrainLat) before scoring a manual-label holdout, Mindboggle-101. They then trained nnU-Net on 1,000 lower-risk cases, 1,000 random cases, and 1,000 higher-risk cases. The lower-risk model beat the random one by 3.2 to 3.7 macro Dice points on all three external cohorts. The higher-risk model trailed random by more than 20 points.

Where it falls short

  • The labels inherit FreeSurfer conventions. Two of the three validation cohorts use FreeSurfer-derived references, so the largest gains sit inside the same convention the model was trained on. On Mindboggle-101, the only manual-label cohort, keeping the lowest-risk quarter helped less than on BrainLat.
  • R is a rank within the release, not a probability of error. A HighConf case can still have a wrong boundary on a small structure, and the gains on 16 subcortical regions are smaller than on the whole brain.
  • Lower-risk and random training sets also differ in which OpenNeuro sources they draw from, so part of the training gain may come from source mix rather than label quality.
  • There are no disease labels, and age, sex and scanner fields are incomplete, so the authors rule out fairness analyses.
  • The committee model weights for SwinUNETR and UNETR are not part of the release. You get their outputs on these 35,838 scans, but if you want Q5 to Q7 on your own data you need to bring your own committee.

What a viewer or clinic shop can take from it

If you build annotation tools or segmentation products, you already live with generated labels. Copy the release format: every auto-generated mask in your pipeline could carry the same kind of record: which model made it, what the source and license were, how two other models voted, and a handful of cheap geometry checks. In a DICOM viewer that becomes a review queue sorted by risk, where an annotator opens the Flagged cases first and skips the HighConf ones, or a training job that drops the top quarter by default. The QC module takes NIfTI folders, and the geometry and intensity checks (Q1 to Q4) run without a committee, so you can try them on your own outputs. Q2 needs more than one scan per source.

For brain work specifically, OpenBrain gives you a large CC0 pretraining or distillation set with the bad tail already marked. The metadata alone is 60 MB, and you can pull one OpenNeuro dataset at a time instead of the full 226 GB.

Code and license

The code is on GitHub at lanqz7766/openbrain under MIT: the seven checks, percentile conversion and tiering, the three training selections, and the evaluation scripts. The data is on Hugging Face at lanqz7766/OpenBrain under CC0 1.0, with a 64-case unpacked sample and one tar per source dataset. Source scans come only from OpenNeuro datasets with CC0-compatible terms. The authors excluded 2,620 audited cases, including those with non-CC0 licenses or unclear redistribution rights. ModernSurfer, the primary labeler, is a separate project under Apache 2.0. The release is for research, not diagnosis or treatment planning.

Paper: arXiv:2611.05348 · Code: github.com/lanqz7766/openbrain (MIT) · Data: huggingface.co/datasets/lanqz7766/OpenBrain (CC0 1.0)

title: Exoplanet Exploration Using Artificial Intelligence
partialText:
Hunting worlds beyond our solar system.

Introduction: The Search for Worlds Beyond Our Solar System

For centuries, humanity has wondered whether we are alone in the universe. Are there other planets like Earth? Could life exist somewhere beyond our solar system? Are there distant worlds with oceans, atmospheres and conditions suitable for biological activity?

Today, these questions are no longer restricted to science fiction. They are the subject of one of the most exciting areas of modern astronomy: exoplanet exploration.

An exoplanet, or extrasolar planet, is a planet that orbits a star outside our solar system. Since the discovery of the first confirmed exoplanets around a Sun-like star in 1995, astronomers have identified thousands of these distant worlds.

The discovery process has evolved considerably. Early observations relied heavily on traditional astronomical techniques and manual analysis. Space missions such as NASA’s Kepler and Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) subsequently transformed the field by collecting enormous quantities of astronomical observations.

However, collecting data is only one part of the challenge. Extracting meaningful scientific information from millions of observations requires sophisticated computational techniques.

This is where Artificial Intelligence (AI) comes into play.

Modern AI systems can identify subtle patterns in stellar brightness, distinguish genuine planetary signals from astronomical noise, analyse atmospheric spectra and accelerate the interpretation of observations from powerful telescopes.

AI is gradually transforming exoplanet exploration from a largely observation-driven process into an intelligent, data-driven scientific discovery pipeline.

What Are Exoplanets?

Exoplanets are planets located outside our solar system. They orbit stars other than the Sun and exhibit an extraordinary diversity of physical characteristics.

Some are enormous gas giants orbiting extremely close to their host stars. Others are rocky planets, potentially containing liquid water or atmospheres.

Scientists have identified several broad categories:

  • Hot Jupiters: Massive gas giants orbiting extremely close to their host stars.
  • Super-Earths: Planets larger than Earth but generally smaller than Neptune. The term describes their size or mass, not necessarily their surface conditions.
  • Mini-Neptunes: Planets smaller than Neptune that may possess substantial gaseous envelopes.
  • Terrestrial planets: Rocky worlds with compositions potentially similar to Mercury, Venus, Earth or Mars.
  • Ocean worlds: Candidate planets that may contain substantial quantities of water, although their actual surface conditions remain difficult to establish.

One particularly interesting concept is the habitable zone.

The habitable zone is the region around a star where temperatures could theoretically permit liquid water to exist on a planet’s surface, assuming suitable atmospheric conditions.

However, being located in the habitable zone does not automatically make a planet habitable. Atmospheric composition, planetary magnetic fields, geological activity, stellar radiation and climate conditions also influence habitability.

The ultimate objective is not simply to discover Earth-sized planets. It is to understand their physical properties, atmospheric composition and potential to support life.

Why Is Exoplanet Exploration Important?

The search for exoplanets helps scientists investigate some fundamental questions:

Understanding planetary formation

Why do some stars have multiple planets while others appear to have none? How do planetary systems evolve? Why are some planets located extremely close to their host stars?

Discovering potentially habitable worlds

Scientists are particularly interested in rocky planets orbiting within the habitable zones of their stars. Studying these planets could help us understand whether Earth-like environments are common throughout the galaxy.

Understanding atmospheric chemistry

A planet’s atmosphere contains valuable information about its composition, temperature, clouds and atmospheric processes. Certain combinations of atmospheric gases could provide clues about biological or geological activity.

Investigating the possibility of extraterrestrial life

One of the long-term goals is identifying potential biosignatures: chemical or physical observations that could indicate biological processes.

Importantly, detecting a potentially interesting gas is not sufficient evidence of life. Scientists must investigate alternative non-biological explanations and consider the planet’s complete environment.

How Do Scientists Detect Exoplanets?

Directly observing an exoplanet is extremely difficult. Most planets are faint compared with their host stars, and their apparent separation from those stars is often incredibly small.

Astronomers therefore use indirect detection techniques to identify planets through their effects on the light or motion of their host stars.

The major detection methods include the following.

Transit Photometry

The transit method is one of the most successful techniques for discovering exoplanets.

When a planet passes between its host star and an observer, it blocks a small fraction of the star’s light. This produces a temporary reduction in the star’s observed brightness.

By continuously monitoring stellar brightness, astronomers can identify these periodic reductions.

A simplified relationship is:

Where:

  • δ (Transit Depth): The fractional dimming or drop in a star’s brightness observed when an orbiting planet passes directly in front of it.
  • R_p: The radius of the orbiting planet (exoplanet).
  • R_s: The radius of the host star.

For example, when an Earth-sized planet transits a Sun-sized star, the reduction in brightness is approximately 0.0084%, an extremely small signal.

Repeated dips can reveal the planet’s orbital period. Combined with information about the host star, the observations can help estimate the planet’s radius and orbital characteristics.

Where AI helps: Deep learning models analyse stellar light curves to identify these tiny brightness variations, even when the observations contain instrumental noise, stellar variability or other astronomical phenomena.

Radial Velocity Method

A planet does not simply orbit its star. Both the planet and star orbit their common centre of mass.

As a result, the star experiences a small periodic movement towards and away from Earth.

This movement produces subtle changes in the star’s observed spectral lines through the Doppler effect.

Astronomers measure these variations to estimate the planet’s minimum mass and orbital properties.

Where AI helps: Machine learning can identify weak periodic velocity signals, distinguish planetary signals from stellar activity and analyse complex stellar spectra.

Direct Imaging

Direct imaging attempts to capture light from the planet itself.

This is challenging because the host star can be millions or billions of times brighter than the planet.

Advanced telescopes use techniques such as coronagraphy and specialised image processing to suppress starlight and isolate planetary signals.

Where AI helps: Computer vision and deep learning can improve image processing, identify faint planetary companions and distinguish genuine planetary signals from imaging artefacts.

Gravitational Microlensing

Gravitational microlensing occurs when the gravitational field of a foreground star magnifies the light from a background star.

If the foreground star has a planet, the planet can produce an additional characteristic distortion in the observed brightness.

AI-based time-series analysis can help identify these complex, short-lived signals in large observational datasets.

Transit Timing Variations

When multiple planets interact gravitationally, their transit times may deviate from the expected periodic schedule.

These variations can provide information about planets that are difficult to detect through conventional transit observations.

Machine learning can help identify subtle timing patterns and support the analysis of interacting planetary systems.

How Artificial Intelligence Is Transforming Exoplanet Discovery

Traditional machine learning approaches generally relied on manually engineered features extracted from astronomical observations.

For example, an astronomer might calculate the depth, duration and frequency of a transit signal before passing these features into a classification algorithm.

Modern AI systems can learn much more complex representations directly from the observations.

The evolution can be understood through five major developments.

Traditional Machine Learning

Algorithms such as:

  • Support Vector Machines (SVM)
  • Random Forest
  • Gradient Boosting
  • XGBoost
  • Logistic Regression

can classify astronomical observations using extracted features.

They remain useful for structured datasets containing planetary radius estimates, orbital periods, stellar properties and signal characteristics.

However, these approaches often depend on extensive feature engineering and may struggle to capture complex patterns directly from raw observations.

Deep Learning for Stellar Light Curves

Deep learning has significantly changed how astronomers analyse stellar brightness measurements.

A light curve is essentially a time-series representation of how a star’s brightness changes over time.

Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) can learn local patterns in these signals, including the characteristic shape of planetary transits.

Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), particularly LSTMs and GRUs, can model temporal dependencies.

More recently, Transformer architectures have introduced attention mechanisms that can capture relationships across longer sequences.

These models can help identify:

  • Weak transit signals.
  • Multiple planets orbiting the same star.
  • Irregular transit patterns.
  • Stellar variability.
  • Instrumental noise and observational artefacts.

One important development is NASA’s ExoMiner, a deep learning framework designed to distinguish genuine exoplanets from false positives.

Its successor, ExoMiner++, extends the approach to Kepler and TESS data.

This demonstrates how AI can move beyond simple classification and become an important component of the scientific validation process.

Self-Supervised Learning and Astronomical Foundation Models

One of the most promising developments in modern AI is self-supervised learning.

Astronomical datasets are enormous, but carefully labelled observations are relatively limited.

Supervised learning requires labelled examples, such as confirmed planets and known false positives. Obtaining these labels can require extensive astronomical analysis and follow-up observations.

Self-supervised learning offers an alternative.

Instead of requiring every observation to have a manually assigned label, a model learns useful representations from large quantities of unlabelled astronomical data.

For example, a model could be trained to:

  1. Predict missing sections of a stellar light curve.
  2. Reconstruct corrupted observations.
  3. Identify relationships between different segments of a time series.
  4. Learn representations of stellar variability.
  5. Detect unusual patterns that differ from previously observed behaviour.

These learned representations can subsequently be fine-tuned for specific tasks, such as planetary transit detection, stellar classification or anomaly identification.

This creates an opportunity to develop astronomical foundation models.

Such models could potentially learn general-purpose representations from different astronomical datasets, including photometry, spectroscopy and imaging.

However, astronomical foundation models are an emerging research direction rather than a single established solution for all exoplanet discovery tasks.

Multimodal AI: Combining Different Astronomical Observations

A planet cannot be fully understood through a single observation.

Transit photometry provides information about planetary size and orbital period. Radial velocity observations help estimate mass. Spectroscopy reveals atmospheric properties.

These observations provide complementary information.

Multimodal AI aims to combine different data modalities into a unified representation.

For example, a multimodal model could process:

  • Stellar light curves.
  • Radial velocity measurements.
  • Stellar spectra.
  • Planetary atmospheric spectra.
  • Telescope images.
  • Stellar and planetary metadata.

The resulting system could help astronomers develop a more complete understanding of a planetary system.

A particularly interesting possibility is cross-modal learning, where information from one observational modality helps interpret another.

For example, stellar properties and planetary orbital parameters can provide useful context when interpreting atmospheric observations.

Physics-Informed Machine Learning

Astronomy is fundamentally governed by physical laws.

A purely data-driven model may identify statistical patterns without necessarily respecting the underlying physics.

Physics-informed machine learning combines scientific knowledge with modern AI architectures.

For exoplanet research, this could involve incorporating:

  • Kepler’s laws of planetary motion.
  • Orbital mechanics.
  • Stellar physics.
  • Radiative transfer.
  • Atmospheric chemistry.
  • Conservation laws.

For example, a neural network could predict a planetary transit signal while a physics-based component ensures that its predicted orbital behaviour remains physically plausible.

This approach can improve interpretability, reduce dependence on labelled data and help prevent physically unrealistic predictions.

AI-Powered Atmospheric Characterization: Looking for Signs of Life

Discovering a planet is only the beginning. Understanding its atmosphere is one of the most important challenges in modern exoplanet science.

When a planet transits its host star, a small fraction of the starlight may pass through its atmosphere.

Different atmospheric molecules absorb light at specific wavelengths, producing characteristic features in the observed spectrum.

This technique is called transmission spectroscopy.

Astronomers can also study atmospheric properties using emission spectroscopy during secondary eclipses and direct imaging observations.

The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) has significantly expanded the capabilities of exoplanet atmospheric characterization through its infrared observations.

AI-Based Spectral Analysis

Atmospheric spectra can contain thousands of data points and complex overlapping absorption features.

Traditional atmospheric retrieval techniques often involve computationally expensive Bayesian inference procedures.

AI can accelerate parts of this process.

Deep learning models can be trained on synthetic atmospheric spectra generated using physical simulations.

These models can learn relationships between atmospheric parameters and observed spectral features.

For example, an AI model could estimate:

  • Water vapour (H₂O).
  • Carbon dioxide (CO₂).
  • Methane (CH₄).
  • Carbon monoxide (CO).
  • Temperature profiles.
  • Cloud properties.
  • Atmospheric pressure.

The model can then provide an initial estimate of atmospheric properties, which can be investigated using more rigorous physical and statistical methods.

Neural Networks for Atmospheric Retrieval

Atmospheric retrieval attempts to infer the physical and chemical properties of an atmosphere from observed spectral data.

A conventional approach repeatedly simulates atmospheric spectra for different combinations of planetary parameters and compares them with observations.

This process can require substantial computational resources.

Machine learning can be used to build surrogate models that approximate expensive atmospheric forward simulations.

A simplified architecture looks like this:

Input:

Observed atmospheric spectrum.

AI model:

A neural network trained on simulated atmospheric spectra.

Output:

Estimated atmospheric properties, such as molecular abundances, temperature and cloud characteristics.

Bayesian inference can then be used to estimate uncertainty and investigate competing atmospheric explanations.

Recent research is also developing machine-learning-ready datasets specifically for atmospheric retrieval, demonstrating the growing importance of AI in this field.

Searching for Biosignatures

One of the most fascinating applications of atmospheric analysis is the search for biosignatures.

Certain atmospheric gases, including oxygen, ozone and methane, can be scientifically interesting when considered in the right planetary context.

However, no individual molecule automatically confirms the presence of life.

AI can help identify combinations of atmospheric signals, investigate unusual chemical patterns and compare observations with simulated planetary environments.

The objective is to identify potentially interesting atmospheric conditions for further scientific investigation, not to declare that extraterrestrial life has been discovered.

Generative AI and Agentic AI in Exoplanet Research

Generative AI and agentic AI introduce another layer of possibilities.

While conventional machine learning models generally perform specific prediction tasks, AI agents can coordinate multiple tools, retrieve information, execute analytical workflows and assist researchers with complex investigations.

Consider a research workflow in which an astronomer wants to investigate a newly identified planetary candidate.

An AI-powered scientific assistant could coordinate several specialised components:

1. Data Retrieval Agent

Retrieves relevant stellar observations, light curves and planetary metadata from public astronomical archives.

2. Signal Analysis Agent

Uses trained deep learning models to analyse transit signals and identify potential planetary candidates.

3. Validation Agent

Checks possible false-positive explanations, including eclipsing binary systems and instrumental artefacts.

4. Atmospheric Analysis Agent

Retrieves available spectral observations and runs atmospheric analysis models.

5. Scientific Literature Agent

Searches relevant research papers and compares the candidate with previously studied planetary systems.

6. Research Synthesis Agent

Combines the findings, identifies uncertainties and prepares a structured scientific report.

The overall workflow could be represented as:

Data Retrieval → Signal Detection → Candidate Validation → Planetary Characterization → Atmospheric Analysis → Scientific Reporting.

An important distinction is that an AI agent should not independently confirm the existence of a planet or make claims about extraterrestrial life.

Scientific validation still requires reliable observations, physical modelling, independent verification and expert review.

Agentic AI is best understood as an orchestration and research-assistance layer around validated scientific tools.

Building a Modern AI Pipeline for Exoplanet Discovery

Let’s bring these concepts together into a modern AI-powered exoplanet discovery architecture.

A practical architecture can be divided into six stages.

Stage 1: Astronomical Data Collection

Collect observations from publicly accessible sources, including:

  • NASA Kepler mission.
  • NASA TESS mission.
  • NASA Exoplanet Archive.
  • Mikulski Archive for Space Telescopes (MAST).
  • European Space Agency (ESA) astronomical archives.

The data can include stellar brightness measurements, observation timestamps, stellar metadata and spectroscopic measurements.

Stage 2: Data Preprocessing

Astronomical observations contain noise and unwanted variations.

Preprocessing may involve:

  • Missing-value handling.
  • Instrumental artefact detection.
  • Stellar variability analysis.
  • Detrending.
  • Normalization.
  • Outlier detection.
  • Quality filtering.

Care must be taken not to remove genuine transit signals during detrending.

Stage 3: AI-Based Signal Detection

Different models can be applied depending on the nature of the data.

AI techniqueApplicationCNNDetecting transit patterns in light curvesLSTM / GRUModelling temporal dependenciesTransformersLearning long-range time-series patternsAutoencodersAnomaly detection and signal reconstructionXGBoostClassification using engineered featuresSelf-supervised learningLearning representations from unlabelled observationsPhysics-informed MLIncorporating physical constraints

The output is a set of potential planetary candidates with associated confidence scores.

Stage 4: Candidate Validation

Not every brightness reduction indicates a planet.

Possible false positives include:

  • Eclipsing binary stars.
  • Background eclipsing binaries.
  • Instrumental noise.
  • Stellar activity.
  • Other astrophysical phenomena.

Deep learning models can help distinguish these possibilities.

For example, ExoMiner++ demonstrates how AI can assist in the validation of planetary candidates identified in large photometric datasets.

Stage 5: Planetary and Atmospheric Characterization

Once a candidate is validated, additional observations can help estimate:

  • Planetary radius.
  • Planetary mass.
  • Orbital period.
  • Orbital eccentricity.
  • Equilibrium temperature.
  • Atmospheric composition.
  • Potential cloud and haze properties.

Machine learning, Bayesian inference and physics-based simulations can work together during this stage.

Stage 6: Scientific Interpretation

The final stage combines model predictions, observational evidence and scientific knowledge.

Researchers can use AI-assisted systems to:

  • Rank interesting candidates for follow-up observations.
  • Compare planets with known planetary populations.
  • Identify unusual atmospheric signatures.
  • Estimate uncertainties.
  • Prioritize telescope observation time.

The objective is to turn astronomical observations into scientifically testable hypotheses.

Technologies and Frameworks for Building Exoplanet AI Systems

A modern implementation can use a combination of scientific Python libraries, machine learning frameworks and astronomical data tools.

The selection of frameworks depends on the research objective, data modality and computational requirements.

For example, Lightkurve is particularly useful for analysing Kepler and TESS photometric observations, whereas PyTorch can be used to develop custom deep learning models.

Future of Exoplanet Exploration: What Comes Next?

The next generation of astronomical instruments will produce increasingly detailed and extensive datasets.

AI will become increasingly important in processing these observations and helping researchers decide where to focus their attention.

Some important developments to watch include:

Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope

NASA’s Roman Space Telescope will conduct wide-field astronomical surveys and contribute valuable data for exoplanet research, including through its microlensing programme and coronagraph technology demonstrations.

PLATO Mission

The European Space Agency’s PLATO mission is designed to discover and characterize planets around bright, nearby stars, particularly small planets around Sun-like stars.

Atmospheric Characterization with JWST

JWST observations are expanding our understanding of exoplanetary atmospheres, helping researchers investigate molecular composition, temperature and atmospheric structure.

Next-Generation Ground-Based Telescopes

Extremely large telescopes will provide new opportunities for high-resolution observations and detailed characterization of distant planetary systems.

AI-Driven Scientific Discovery

Future AI systems may combine observations from multiple telescopes, identify unexpected astronomical phenomena, suggest follow-up observations and help scientists investigate complex scientific hypotheses.

The long-term possibility is an increasingly automated discovery ecosystem in which AI systems continuously analyse incoming observations and direct researchers towards the most scientifically interesting targets.

Conclusion: From Discovering Planets to Understanding Other Worlds

Exoplanet exploration has evolved significantly since the early days of planetary discovery.

Traditional machine learning introduced automated classification and pattern recognition. Deep learning subsequently enabled more sophisticated analysis of astronomical time series and images.

Today, self-supervised learning, multimodal AI, physics-informed neural networks, Bayesian machine learning and agentic AI are opening new possibilities.

The biggest opportunity is not simply to discover more planets. It is to understand them.

Can we identify rocky planets with potentially suitable atmospheric conditions? Can we analyse their chemical composition more efficiently? Can we distinguish biological signals from non-biological processes?

These questions remain challenging, but modern AI is providing astronomers with increasingly powerful tools to investigate them.

Perhaps the most exciting future is one in which AI does not merely help us process astronomical observations but also helps us discover scientific patterns that humans might otherwise overlook.

We may not yet know whether life exists beyond Earth, but with the combination of advanced telescopes, scientific computing and artificial intelligence, we are getting better at knowing where to look.

References

These are useful resources for further reading and linking within your blog:

  1. NASA — ExoMiner++: AI-powered exoplanet discovery (2026).
  2. NASA — Deep Learning Method Adds 301 Planets to Kepler’s Total Count.
  3. Machine Learning-Ready Dataset for Exoplanet Atmospheric Retrieval (2025).
  4. NASA ExoMiner — Open-source GitHub repository.
